notes.short: Nineveh pictured as a lions’ lair full of prey
notes.about: The prophet asks where the lions’ lair has gone, the den where lion, lioness and cubs prowled with nothing to fear, and the lion filled its dens with the kill. The lions are Nineveh’s rulers and warriors, who tore the nations and stored the plunder in the city; verse 13 applies the picture to her.

figure.name: Allegory
figure.means: Nineveh, home of Assyria’s kings and warriors, who preyed on the nations like lions and filled the city with their plunder

notes.evidence: Clarke calls verses 11 and 12 a very beautiful allegory, explained and applied to Nineveh in verse 13. Keil: the city is the lions’ dwelling, the point being the plundering lust of its rulers and warriors, and verse 12 keeps the figure. Calvin: Nineveh was like a den of lions, and the comparison shows Assyrian cruelty. Fausset (Jamieson, Fausset and Brown): the lions typify its warriors.

cites.quote: This description is succeeded by a very beautiful and expressive allegory, Nah 2:11-12 ; which is immediately explained, and applied to the city of Nineveh, Nah 2:13 .

Under the same figure Nah 2:12 describes the tyranny and predatory lust of the Assyrians in their wars.

cites.quote: For Nineveh was not only the receptacle of robbers but was also like a den of lions. And the Prophet more fully expresses the barbarous cruelty of the Assyrians by comparing them to lions, than if he had simply called them lions.

Nineveh, the seat of empire of the rapacious and destructive warriors of various ranks, typified by the "lions," "young lions," "old lion" ... It was as full of spoils of all nations as a lion's den is of remains of its prey.

notes.short: Nineveh pictured as a harlot put to shame
notes.about: Nineveh is pictured as a harlot skilled in sorcery, who lures and betrays nations. The LORD then puts her to shame as a harlot: her skirts lifted over her face, her nakedness shown to the nations, filth thrown on her, until all who see her recoil and no one grieves for her.

figure.name: Allegory
figure.words: the many harlotries of the harlot
figure.means: Nineveh’s craft and allurements, by which she drew nations under her power; some read it as leading them into idolatry

notes.evidence: Calvin says the prophet compares Nineveh to a harlot because she ensnared nations by craft and allurements as well as by force. Clarke: the city is shown under the emblem of a beautiful harlot enticing the nations. Fausset (Jamieson, Fausset and Brown): as a harlot’s looks allure, so nations were tempted to trust Assyria. Keil: her coquetry is repaid by the uncovering of her nakedness.
notes.limit: The writers differ on what the harlotry stands for: two take it as crafty dealings that lured nations into her power, one as leading them into idolatry. One takes the shaming of verses 6 and 7 as said in plainer terms.

cites.quote: Hence he compares Nineveh to a harlot. ... The Prophet then makes the city Nineveh to be like a harlot for this reason, — because it had not only brought under its power neighboring nations by threats and terrors, and also by cruelty, but because it had ensnared many by oblique arts and fraudulent means, by captious dealings and allurements.

Above, the Ninevites were represented under the emblem of a lion tearing all to pieces; here they are represented under the emblem of a beautiful harlot or public prostitute, enticing all men to her, inducing the nations to become idolatrous, and, by thus perverting them, rendering them also objects of the Divine wrath.

notes.short: Nineveh’s fortresses are ripe fig trees
notes.about: Nineveh’s fortresses are said to be fig trees loaded with the first ripe figs: shake the tree and the fruit drops straight into the eater’s mouth. So the strongholds the city trusted would fall to the enemy at the first blow, with hardly any effort.

figure.name: Metaphor
figure.words: All your fortresses are fig trees with the first ripe figs
figure.means: Nineveh’s strongholds: ready to fall to the enemy at the first assault, as ripe figs drop when the tree is shaken

notes.evidence: Clarke calls it a very expressive metaphor: ripe figs drop at the least shake, and so the fortresses would be abandoned at the first alarm. Calvin calls it a very apt similitude: the strongholds would fall of themselves. Keil says the point of the comparison is the ease with which the enemy would take the castles; Fausset (Jamieson, Fausset and Brown), the speed and ease of the capture of Nineveh.

cites.quote: The effects of the consternation into which the Ninevites were cast by the assault on their city are here pointed out by a very expressive metaphor; the first-ripe figs, when at full maturity, fell from the tree with the least shake; and so, at the first shake or consternation, all the fortresses of Nineveh were abandoned

cites.quote: for all things, he says, will of themselves fall, even without being much assailed. And he employs a very apposite similitude, “Thy fortifications,” he says, “which thou thinkest to be very strong, shall be like figs; for when the fruit is ripe, and any comes to the tree, as soon as he touches it or any of the branches, the figs will fall off themselves.”

All the fortifications of Nineveh are like fig-trees with early figs ... which fall into the mouth of the eater when the trees are shaken. The tertium compar. is the facility with which the castles will be taken and destroyed by the enemy assaulting them

notes.about: The prophet turns to the locust again and again. The sword will consume Nineveh like the young locust, however many she makes herself. Her guards and scribes are like locusts that settle on the walls on a cold day and fly off when the sun rises, and no one knows where. Her great numbers will vanish.

figure.name: Simile
figure.words: Your guards are like the swarming locust
figure.means: Nineveh’s many guards and officers: as numerous as locusts, yet gone as suddenly when trouble comes, leaving no trace

notes.evidence: E. B. Pusey (Barnes’ Notes): the prophet expands his metaphor into a likeness, locusts stiff with cold picturing the helplessness of Nineveh’s mightiest, and their flight their entire disappearance. Keil: the figure takes a new turn, the Assyrian army a swarm that perishes without a trace. Calvin and Fausset (Jamieson, Fausset and Brown): the vast multitude will vanish away.
notes.limit: The writers differ on verse 16: some take the locust that strips the land and flies away as the enemy army, others as Nineveh’s own multitude scattering.

cites.quote: What he had said summarily under metaphor, the prophet expands in a likeness. ... The stiffness of the locusts through the cold, when they lie motionless, heaps upon heaps, hidden out of sight, is a striking image of the helplessness of Nineveh's mightiest in the day of her calamity; then, by a different part of their history, he pictures their entire disappearance.

cites.quote: It is true that in the following sentences the locusts are used figuratively for the Assyrians, or the inhabitants of Nineveh; but it is also by no means a rare thing for prophets to give a new turn and application to a figure or simile. ... the Assyrian army, which is compared to a swarm of locusts, so that its place is known no more ... i.e., has perished without leaving a trace behind.

cites.quote: From these words we may learn what the Prophet before meant, when he said that the Assyrians were like locusts or chafers ... he points out another reason for the comparison ... that the Assyrians, while they were almost innumerable, gloried in their great number, — and also, that this vast multitude would vanish away.

Cold deprives the locust of the power of flight; so they alight in cold weather and at night, but when warmed by the sun soon "flee away." So shall the Assyrian multitudes suddenly disappear, not leaving a trace behind
